szoveg_eredeti:
Over the last year, Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.47%)(BRKB +0.53%) has become a surprising participant in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Under CEO Greg Abel, the investment conglomerate has expanded its investment in Alphabet (GOOGL -0.98%) (GOOG -0.96%), signaling that certain technology companies can fit Berkshire's portfolio criteria.

Berkshire ended September with roughly $377.4 billion in cash and Treasury bills, providing more than enough financial flexibility for future investments. My prediction is ASML Holding (ASML -0.13%) could become Berkshire's next AI stock.

While ASML doesn't look like a traditional Warren Buffett investment on the surface, its monopoly-like market position, pricing power, and predictable cash flow make it a compelling candidate.

Buffett spent his career emphasizing the importance of an economic moat, or a durable competitive advantage that protects a company's profitability from rivals. For some companies, those advantages come from brand equity. For others, it comes from network effects, switching costs, or intellectual property (IP).

ASML's moat is impressive because the company is something of a monopoly. ASML is the world's only commercial manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These are essential for producing advanced semiconductors.

Customers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Samsung, and Intel rely on ASML's equipment to manufacture cutting-edge chips. Replicating ASML's technology would be exceptionally difficult, even for a well-funded competitor. This creates enormous barriers to entry and supports ASML's pricing power.

Moreover, ASML doesn't need to predict whether Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, or another chip designer will dominate the AI market. As long as semiconductor manufacturers continue to invest in new architectures, ASML is positioned to benefit. This model resembles the tollbooth-style businesses Buffett appreciates.

Another element of Buffett's investment philosophy is the ability to forecast a company's future earnings and cash flow. ASML offers a compelling example.

During the third quarter, the company generated 11.7 billion euros in revenue, alongside approximately 5 billion euros in net income. The company's gross margin was 57.5%. Management guided for full-year revenue between 44 billion and 45 billion euros, with a gross margin around 56%.

ASML disclosed that some customers are already expressing interest in equipment deliveries scheduled for 2029 and 2030. Management also indicated that its manufacturing capacity for 2027 and 2028 will not fully satisfy anticipated customer demand.

That degree of visibility is valuable because it helps management plan manufacturing expansion, anticipate future revenue, and make more informed capital allocation decisions. For investors, it provides a strong foundation for estimating long-term free cash flow.

ASML's business includes another attractive feature: recurring service revenue and equipment upgrades. As customers operate their lithography machines, ASML can generate additional revenue through maintenance, productivity improvements, and upgrades. These recurring services help diversify revenue beyond new equipment sales.

As of this writing (Nov. 13), ASML trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 23. That's hardly a bargain-basement multiple, particularly for a capital-intensive equipment company exposed to industry spending cycles. However, for a company with ASML's competitive advantages, that valuation could warrant closer examination.

Remember, Berkshire has added to its stake in Alphabet since opening a position in the third quarter of last year. During this time, Alphabet has experienced notable valuation expansion. In some ways, this could suggest that Berkshire is willing to pay a slight premium for exceptional businesses.

Remember, Buffett is hardly a fan of trying to predict which company will develop the next revolutionary technology. The "Oracle of Omaha" supports the businesses that produce indispensable equipment and services everyone else needs to compete.

If current CEO Greg Abel wants to expand Berkshire's AI exposure without betting directly on a hyperscaler or individual chip designer, I think ASML deserves consideration.
